## Overview

::: {.callout-important}
## Focus for Today
This lab introduces the **t-test** - the workhorse of psychological research for comparing means:

- Running independent samples t-tests (between-subjects)
- Running paired samples t-tests (within-subjects)
- Interpreting R output from t.test()
- Choosing the right test for your design
:::

---

## Activity 1: Independent t-test (Lab A vs Lab B Memory) (20 min)

### When to Use an Independent t-test

An **independent samples t-test** compares means from **two different groups** of participants.


::: {.cell}

:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](activity_files/figure-html/lab-comparison-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


### Conceptual Questions

**1. This comparison (Lab A vs Lab B) uses an independent t-test because:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The same participants are in both groups</option><option value='answer'>Different participants are in each group</option><option value=''>We are comparing more than two groups</option><option value=''>There is no control group</option></select>

**2. What are the two groups being compared?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Lab A (abstract words) vs Lab B (concrete words)</option><option value=''>Before vs After</option><option value=''>High vs Low performers</option><option value=''>Morning vs Afternoon sessions</option></select>

**3. What is the dependent variable in this analysis?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Word type (abstract/concrete)</option><option value=''>Lab group</option><option value='answer'>Number of words recalled</option><option value=''>Participant ID</option></select>

### Understanding the R Output

Here's what R output from `t.test()` looks like:

```
	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  mem_total_1 by Lab
t = -2.45, df = 38.2, p-value = 0.019
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.15  -0.21
sample estimates:
mean in group Lab A  mean in group Lab B
               5.40                6.58
```

**4. Looking at the output above, what is the t-statistic?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>38.2</option><option value=''>0.019</option><option value='answer'>-2.45</option><option value=''>-2.15</option></select>

**5. What is the p-value?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>-2.45</option><option value=''>38.2</option><option value='answer'>0.019</option><option value=''>6.58</option></select>

**6. At alpha = 0.05, would we reject the null hypothesis?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Yes, because p < 0.05</option><option value=''>No, because p > 0.05</option><option value=''>Can't tell from this output</option><option value=''>Yes, because t is negative</option></select>

**7. The 95% CI for the difference is [-2.15, -0.21]. What does this tell us?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>The CI doesn't include 0, supporting a real difference</option><option value=''>The CI includes 0, so there's no difference</option><option value=''>Lab B scored lower than Lab A</option><option value=''>The difference is not significant</option></select>

True or False: A negative t-value means the first group has a lower mean than the second. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

## Activity 2: Paired t-test (Pre vs Post Mood) (20 min)

### When to Use a Paired t-test

A **paired samples t-test** compares means from the **same participants** measured twice.


::: {.cell}

:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](activity_files/figure-html/mood-comparison-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672}
:::
:::


### Conceptual Questions

**1. This comparison uses a paired t-test because:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>The same participants are measured at both time points</option><option value=''>Different participants are in each group</option><option value=''>We are comparing more than two groups</option><option value=''>The data is paired with another dataset</option></select>

**2. What is the advantage of a paired design over an independent design?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Easier to recruit participants</option><option value=''>Faster to run</option><option value='answer'>Each person is their own control, reducing individual differences</option><option value=''>No assumptions required</option></select>

**3. In R, how do we specify a paired t-test?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>t.test(x, y, type = 'paired')</option><option value='answer'>t.test(x, y, paired = TRUE)</option><option value=''>paired.t.test(x, y)</option><option value=''>t.test.paired(x, y)</option></select>

### Understanding Paired Output

```
	Paired t-test

data:  mood_pre and mood_post
t = -3.12, df = 42, p-value = 0.003
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -1.52  -0.32
sample estimates:
mean difference
          -0.92
```

**4. The mean difference of -0.92 means:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Pre scores were 0.92 higher than post</option><option value='answer'>Post scores were 0.92 higher than pre</option><option value=''>The groups are 0.92 apart on average</option><option value=''>92% of people improved</option></select>

**5. Is this difference statistically significant at alpha = 0.05?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Yes, p = 0.003 < 0.05</option><option value=''>No, p = 0.003 > 0.05</option><option value=''>Can't tell</option><option value=''>Only marginally significant</option></select>

**6. The degrees of freedom (df) for a paired t-test equals:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>n</option><option value='answer'>n - 1 (number of pairs minus 1)</option><option value=''>n - 2</option><option value=''>n1 + n2 - 2</option></select>

True or False: In a paired t-test, we analyse the difference scores, not the raw scores. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

---

## Activity 3: Interpreting Output (20 min)

### Reading and Reporting t-test Results

Psychologists report t-test results in a specific format. Let's practice!

**Standard format:** t(df) = value, p = value

### Practice Examples

**Example 1:**
```
t = 2.34, df = 28, p-value = 0.027
```

**1. How would you report this result?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>t = 2.34, p = 0.027</option><option value='answer'>t(28) = 2.34, p = .027</option><option value=''>t(2.34) = 28, p = 0.027</option><option value=''>df = 28, t = 2.34</option></select>

**2. Is this result significant at alpha = 0.05?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Yes</option><option value=''>No</option><option value=''>Can't tell</option><option value=''>Marginally significant</option></select>

**Example 2:**
```
t = 1.52, df = 45, p-value = 0.136
```

**3. Is this result significant at alpha = 0.05?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Yes</option><option value='answer'>No</option><option value=''>Can't tell</option><option value=''>Marginally significant</option></select>

**4. What should you conclude?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The groups are definitely the same</option><option value='answer'>We cannot reject the null hypothesis - insufficient evidence of a difference</option><option value=''>The experiment failed</option><option value=''>We need to use a different test</option></select>

### Assumptions of the t-test

**5. Which assumption is about the shape of the data distribution?**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Normality assumption</option><option value=''>Independence assumption</option><option value=''>Homogeneity of variance</option><option value=''>Randomness assumption</option></select>

**6. Welch's t-test is preferred when:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Sample sizes are equal</option><option value=''>Data is normally distributed</option><option value='answer'>Variances may be unequal between groups</option><option value=''>We want a paired test</option></select>

**7. Independence means:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>One person's score doesn't influence another's</option><option value=''>The groups are completely separate</option><option value=''>Variables are uncorrelated</option><option value=''>The test is unbiased</option></select>

True or False: t-tests are robust to mild violations of normality, especially with larger samples. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: If p = 0.06, the result is "almost significant" and we should report it as meaningful. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>

## Activity 4: Choosing the Right Test (20 min)

### Decision Tree Practice

For each scenario, identify whether to use an **independent** or **paired** t-test.

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 1
A researcher measures anxiety levels in 30 participants before and after a relaxation intervention.

**Which t-test?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Independent t-test</option><option value='answer'>Paired t-test</option></select>

**Why?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Different people in each condition</option><option value='answer'>Same people measured twice</option></select>
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 2
Comparing exam scores between students who used Method A vs Method B to study.

**Which t-test?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Independent t-test</option><option value=''>Paired t-test</option></select>

**Why?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Different people in each condition</option><option value=''>Same people measured twice</option></select>
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 3
Testing whether people rate faces as more attractive when the same faces are presented smiling vs neutral.

**Which t-test?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Independent t-test</option><option value='answer'>Paired t-test</option></select>

**Why?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Different people rate different faces</option><option value='answer'>Same people rate both versions of faces</option></select>
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 4
Comparing reaction times between left-handed and right-handed participants.

**Which t-test?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Independent t-test</option><option value=''>Paired t-test</option></select>

**Why?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Handedness is a between-subjects variable</option><option value=''>People switch hands during the experiment</option></select>
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}

### Scenario 5
Each participant completes a task under quiet conditions and under noisy conditions.

**Which t-test?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Independent t-test</option><option value='answer'>Paired t-test</option></select>

**Why?** <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Different people in each condition</option><option value='answer'>Same people tested in both conditions</option></select>
:::

### The Key Question

**To decide which t-test to use, ask yourself:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>How many variables are there?</option><option value=''>Is the data normally distributed?</option><option value='answer'>Are the SAME or DIFFERENT people in each condition?</option><option value=''>What is the sample size?</option></select>

---

## Summary

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Takeaways

**Independent t-test:**
- Compares means from TWO DIFFERENT groups
- Use for between-subjects designs
- df = n1 + n2 - 2

**Paired t-test:**
- Compares means from the SAME people measured twice
- Use for within-subjects designs
- df = n - 1 (number of pairs minus 1)
- More powerful (controls for individual differences)

**Reporting:**
- Format: t(df) = value, p = value
- Include effect size (Cohen's d) when possible
- Report 95% CI for the difference

**Choosing:**
- Ask: "Same people or different people?"
:::
